objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain straight-and-level flight, trim and the outside and instrument references a new learner uses, fly it from the right seat while talking a learner through it, and spot, explain and fix the errors a beginner makes on the first lessons.
why: Straight-and-level is the first of the four fundamentals, and every later maneuver is built as a variation of it [[24:62|AFH 3-1]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. Habits formed in these first hours, good or bad, are the ones that stick, so the instructor has to get the sight picture, the light touch and the outside scan right from the start [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. This is often the first thing a new learner flies, so it is also where you set the tone for the whole course [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

warmup: Think first: on a new learner's first lesson you hand over the controls in cruise. Within a minute the altitude has wandered 150 feet, the heading has crept 20° left, and the learner's eyes have not left the attitude indicator. The learner grips the yoke hard and says it feels twitchy. Which of these problems would you fix first, what would you say, and what did you leave out of the ground briefing that could have prevented all of it?

key_terms.def: Flight in which heading and altitude are maintained. The other fundamentals are variations of it [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
The angle between the airplane's longitudinal axis (nose to tail) and the natural horizon [[24:65|AFH 3-4]].
The angle between the airplane's lateral axis (wingtip to wingtip) and the natural horizon [[24:65|AFH 3-4]].
A misleading horizon that can appear when the natural horizon is obscured or not readily apparent [[24:65|AFH 3-4]] [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]].
Four parts: pitch control with the elevator, bank control with the ailerons, power control with the throttle, and trim to relieve held pressures [[24:66|AFH 3-5]].
Also called the composite method: the learner uses outside references and flight instruments together to set and hold attitudes and performance [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].
A control that offsets a constant control pressure so the airplane holds the attitude without the pilot pushing or pulling [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].
Sensing a flight condition without instruments, through sounds, vibrations and accelerations felt by the body [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].
The ability to sense movement through the body. Useful with visual cues, but relied on alone it leads to disorientation [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].
Making one excessive correction after another because the beginner does not understand instrument lag and precession [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
Becoming absorbed in one task, or one instrument, so that everything else goes unwatched [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].
A routine, usually clearing turns, that makes sure the next maneuver will not proceed into another aircraft's flightpath [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

chunks.title: What straight-and-level is and why it comes first

body.p: Straight-and-level flight is flight in which heading and altitude are maintained. Turns, climbs and descents are all variations of it, and the skill comes from repetition and practice [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. The AFH calls the four fundamentals the foundation for every other flying task, and warns that moving on to advanced maneuvers before they are mastered hinders learning [[24:62|AFH 3-1]].

Purpose: for you as the instructor, this is where the learner first learns attitude awareness. Deficiencies in the fundamentals become barriers to learning as the maneuvers get more complex [[24:62|AFH 3-1]]. What good performance looks like: the pilot perceives outside references, takes mental snapshots of the flight instruments, and makes timely, proportional corrections for slight unintended turns, climbs and descents [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

The physics you will explain on the ground: in steady flight the opposing forces cancel. Lift and weight are equal to each other, and thrust and drag are equal to each other [[1:99|PHAK 5-2]]. To stay in steady, level flight, lift must equal weight and thrust must equal drag [[1:261|PHAK 11-5]]. Straight-and-level can be flown across a wide range of speeds; the pilot coordinates angle of attack and thrust, so slower flight needs a higher angle of attack to keep lift equal to weight [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]].

bullets: With power held constant, airspeed stays essentially constant in straight-and-level flight [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].
Add power and the airplane speeds up and starts to climb unless the angle of attack is reduced, timed with the speed change [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]].
Intentional airspeed changes with power, while holding straight-and-level, build proficiency [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].
Flaps, landing gear and other drag devices also create pitching moments; cover them in each airplane checkout [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

callout.text: Two numbers to hold, heading and altitude; one picture to hold, the nose and wingtips on the horizon.

check.q: Your learner reduces power in level flight and holds the same pitch attitude. What will the airplane do, and what must the learner do to stay level?
check.a: It slows, lift becomes less than weight and it starts to descend. To hold altitude the learner must raise the angle of attack and accept the lower speed, staying alert near the critical angle of attack [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]].

chunks.title: Attitude flying: pitch, bank, power and trim

body.p: An airplane's attitude is the angle between one of its axes and the natural horizon. Pitch attitude uses the longitudinal axis, nose to tail; bank attitude uses the lateral axis, wingtip to wingtip. Yaw is relative to the direction of flight, not to the horizon [[24:65|AFH 3-4]].

In visual conditions the pilot judges attitude by looking at the wings and cowling against the natural horizon. If no horizon can be seen, because of clouds, whiteout, haze over the ocean or night over a dark ocean, it is IMC for practical and safety purposes [[24:65|AFH 3-4]].

head: Component
Control
What it does
rows: Pitch control
Elevator
Raises and lowers the nose against the natural horizon or the instruments [[24:66|AFH 3-5]]
Bank control
Ailerons
Sets the bank angle about the longitudinal axis [[24:66|AFH 3-5]]
Power control
Throttle
Sets a thrust, or changes it to meet a specific objective [[24:66|AFH 3-5]]
Trim control
Trim wheel or switch
Relieves the pressures held after the attitude is set [[24:66|AFH 3-5]]

body.p: Yaw control (rudder) is used to cancel yaw from things like adverse yaw and propeller effects [[24:66|AFH 3-5]]. In level flight, 'increase the back pressure' or 'increase pitch attitude' means raise the nose against the natural horizon, and 'decrease pitch attitude' means lower it. The primary reference is the natural horizon [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

callout.text: Use the AFH words in the air the same way you used them on the ground. A learner who hears 'raise the nose to the horizon' and 'add back pressure' as two different things will hesitate.

check.q: A learner asks why yaw is not part of 'attitude' the way pitch and bank are. What do you answer?
check.a: Pitch and bank are measured against the natural horizon; yaw is an angle relative to the airplane's direction of flight, not to the horizon [[24:65|AFH 3-4]]. The rudder is used to cancel unwanted yaw [[24:66|AFH 3-5]].

body.p: The AFH describes every control from the pilot's frame of reference [[24:63|AFH 3-2]]:

bullets: Back pressure: the nose rotates toward the pilot about the pitch axis, a movement from the feet toward the head [[24:63|AFH 3-2]].
Right aileron pressure: the right wing lowers, from the head toward the right hip [[24:63|AFH 3-2]].
Right rudder pressure: the nose yaws right, from the left shoulder toward the right shoulder [[24:63|AFH 3-2]].

body.p: Teach pressures, not positions. Control resistance rises with airspeed, and what matters is the pressure that gives the result, not how far the surface moves [[24:64|AFH 3-3]]. Hold the yoke or stick lightly with the fingers; a closed palm grip loses the sensitive feel that the learner needs, and the AFH suggests dealing with it at the very start of training [[24:64|AFH 3-3]]. Heels rest on the floor with the balls of the feet on the pedals, legs relaxed, and the opposite pedal relaxed as one is pressed [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].

Bank corrections use coordinated aileron and rudder; using either one alone is not correct and makes precise control hard. A trimmed airplane in smooth air needs almost no control pressure in straight-and-level, so the learner should not form the habit of moving the controls without a reason [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

Feel. The AFH calls sensing a flight condition without instruments 'feeling the airplane': airflow noise, engine and propeller sound, vibration and accelerations felt in the seat [[24:64|AFH 3-3]]. Your job is to teach the difference between merely noticing these cues and perceiving and reacting to them [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].

bullets: Rising airflow noise usually means airspeed increasing and pitch decreasing [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].
In a fixed-pitch airplane, engine sound decreases as pitch increases [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].
Being pushed sideways in the seat signals a slip or skid [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].
Feel alone, without visual information, ends in disorientation and loss of control [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].

callout.text: Fingertips on the yoke, heels on the floor, eyes on the horizon.

check.q: Your learner corrects a small heading drift by pressing rudder alone and leaving the wings slightly banked. Why does the AFH call this wrong?
check.a: Using aileron or rudder independently is not correct and makes precise control difficult; bank corrections need coordinated aileron and rudder [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

chunks.title: Trim: set the attitude, then trim out the pressure

body.p: Trim offsets a constant control pressure. Elevator trim nulls the pressure needed to hold a pitch attitude, which frees the pilot's attention for other tasks [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]. Nearly all light airplanes have at least adjustable elevator trim; rudder and aileron trim appear as airplanes get bigger and more complex [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

How it works, for the learner who asks: on a typical small airplane a trim tab on the elevator's trailing edge is moved by a trim wheel or crank. Full nose-down trim moves the tab fully up; the airflow then pushes the elevator's trailing edge down, the tail rises and the nose goes down [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]]. Whenever power, pitch attitude or configuration changes, the airplane needs retrimming [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]. Many small airplanes also have a ground adjustable rudder tab, bent on the ground by trial and error [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]].

head: Step
What the learner does
rows: 1. Set and hold
Establish the attitude and hold it with control pressure; let the airspeed settle [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]
2. Rudder (if adjustable)
With constant speed and pitch, hold the wings level with aileron while trimming out rudder pressure [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]
3. Elevator
Trim out the elevator pressure; rudder, elevator, then aileron is the AFH sequence [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]
4. Aileron (if adjustable)
Trim out any aileron pressure that remains [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]
5. Confirm
The airplane holds the attitude with no pilot pressure; any force felt should come from a deliberate input [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]

callout.text: Common trim error: overcontrolling with trim, or flying the airplane with the trim wheel. The AFH says this fault shows up even in experienced pilots. Attitude first, held with pressure, then trim [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

body.p: Trimming rudder and aileron while the airspeed is still changing just adds workload and distraction, and in many propeller airplanes trimming the rudder at varying speeds is impractical [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

check.q: Your learner rolls the trim wheel to raise the nose instead of using back pressure. What do you say?
check.a: Set the attitude with the elevator and hold it with pressure first, then trim the pressure out. Flying the airplane with the trim is a common fault [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

chunks.title: Seat position and the nose sight picture

body.p: Straight-and-level is a matter of consciously fixing a reference point on the airplane against the natural horizon. Those reference points depend on the pilot's seating position, height and posture, so set them up on the ground [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. The pilot sits normally, with the seat adjusted to see adequately over the panel while able to fully depress the rudder pedals without straining or reaching [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

bullets: A flight instructor may use a dry erase marker or removable tape to mark reference lines on the windshield or cowling [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
Vertical lines: best made on the ground, with the airplane on a marked centerline and the learner seated in the proper position [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
Horizontal lines: best made in flight, for example in slow flight and cruise configurations; there are several because different pitch attitudes are needed [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
The horizon reference point is the same at any altitude, even though the horizon is farther away as you climb [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
These aids are needed only for a short time, until the learner knows where and when to look [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

body.p: Level pitch attitude: properly seated, the learner picks a point toward the nose and keeps it fixed against the natural horizon, then cross-checks the instruments. If the altitude is trending away, readjust the pitch on the horizon first, then cross-check again [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

callout.text: Ask the learner to say where the reference sits in words, for example 'the horizon two fingers above the glareshield'. Forgetting the preselected reference points on later flights is one of the AFH's listed errors [[24:70|AFH 3-9]].

check.q: Why does the AFH want vertical reference lines made on the ground but horizontal ones made in flight?
check.a: Vertical lines can be lined up with a marked centerline while the learner sits in position; the horizontal lines depend on the pitch attitudes actually flown, such as slow flight and cruise [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

chunks.title: Wingtips, heading and flying a straight line

body.p: Straight flight is checked by the wingtips. On a high wing or a low wing, both tips should be level and equally above or below the natural horizon; correct bank with coordinated aileron and rudder. Anytime the wings are banked, the airplane turns [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

Why the wingtips and not the nose: the nose gives only a short horizontal reference line, so small bank deviations go unnoticed. The wingtips make them obvious, and the AFH makes the wingtips the primary reference for a level bank attitude [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]. This also prevents the habit of flying one wing low and holding heading with opposite rudder, a habit that makes every later maneuver harder [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

Pilots tend to look out to one side, usually the left from the left seat. That narrows the view and leads to unconscious control pressure toward that side. Scanning both wingtips is the only positive check for level wings, and it brings traffic, terrain and weather into view too [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

bullets: Flying a line: pick a point on the horizon aligned with a nearer point ahead; if they stay aligned, the airplane tracks the line [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].
A course can also be held by tracking toward a point with glances at the compass or magnetic direction indicator [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].
Surface points do not work over water or flat snow covered ground; use the magnetic heading indication there [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].
Instrument cross-check for bank: the attitude indicator shows the wings against the horizon, and the heading indicator shows whether the heading has drifted [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

check.q: Over a frozen lake your learner cannot find two aligned ground points to fly a line. What does the AFH say to use?
check.a: Surface points do not work over water or flat snow covered surfaces; rely on the magnetic heading indication [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

body.p: The AFH recommends the integrated, or composite, method when introducing basic maneuvers: outside references and flight instruments are both used to establish and maintain attitude and performance [[24:66|AFH 3-5]]. The AIH adds that instrument references should start the first time each new maneuver is introduced, and that the control inputs are the same whichever reference is used [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

head: Element
What the learner does
rows: Control outside
Controls attitude against the natural horizon, with approximately 90 percent of attention outside on references and traffic [[24:66|AFH 3-5]]
Validate inside
Confirms performance on the instruments, applies any correction on the natural horizon, then rechecks [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]
Monitor briefly
Keeps no more than about 10 percent of attention inside, then returns to the outside references [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]

body.p: Scale is why the horizon wins. A pitch change of several inches on the horizon may show as a seemingly insignificant movement on the attitude indicator, and a bank error obvious on the wingtips may be imperceptible on the attitude indicator to a beginner [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. A beginner who flies by the instruments, not understanding instrument lag and gyroscopic precession, ends up chasing them; the natural horizon gives immediate indications many times larger [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

Integrated instruction begins with the first briefing on the flight controls, which covers the instrument indications to expect as well as the outside references [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Learners trained this way build the habit of monitoring their own performance, land better through more precise airspeed control, and start their instrument training with a firm foundation [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. If the learner fixates on the panel, the AFH lets you cover the flight instruments for the first several hours to force outside references [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

callout.text: Tell every learner plainly: this does not prepare you for IMC. Anytime attitude by the natural horizon cannot be established or maintained, it is a genuine emergency [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. VFR flight into IMC is one of the most common causes of fatal accidents [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: Your learner holds altitude well but only by staring at the PFD. Under integrated instruction, what is the fix?
check.a: Return control to the natural horizon, with most attention outside and only brief instrument checks; if the fixation persists, cover the instruments for a time [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

chunks.title: Demonstrating it from the right seat

body.p: The CFI ACS asks you to demonstrate and simultaneously explain (ACS AI.VIII.A.S1). While demonstrating, explain the power settings and attitudes, keep the demonstration in the same order as your explanation, and if the demonstration strays from it, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Avoid extraneous activity so the learner sees only the task [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

Your picture is not the learner's picture. Reference points depend on seating position, height and posture [[24:67|AFH 3-6]], and a side-by-side pilot sits off the airplane's longitudinal axis [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Application: from the right seat your nose reference point sits in a different place from the learner's, so find the learner's point from the left seat on the ground rather than describing your own.
A talk-through you can adapt (each step from the sources):

bullets: 'First we clear the area.' Clearing comes before any training maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
'Cruise power set. Watch how this spot on the cowling sits on the horizon.' The pitch reference stays fixed on the natural horizon [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].
'Now both wingtips: equal distance from the horizon.' The wingtips are the primary bank reference [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].
'Quick look inside: altitude steady, heading steady. Back outside.' Brief checks, no more than about 10 percent of attention inside [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
'I hold the attitude with light pressure, then trim it out.' Attitude first, then trim [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].
'Hands off for a moment: it stays put.' A trimmed airplane needs almost no control pressure in smooth air [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

callout.text: Fly the demonstration to the precision you will expect from the learner. Learners imitate the instructor, so show it exactly the way you want it practiced [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

check.q: During your demonstration the altitude drifts 80 feet while you are talking. What should you do?
check.a: Acknowledge and explain the deviation immediately, because a demonstration that does not match the explanation confuses the learner [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

chunks.title: How to teach it on the first lessons

body.p: This is often the learner's first time on the controls. Anxiety is probably the most significant psychological factor in flight instruction; treat fears as normal and tell learners what to expect [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Keep the first lesson positive and do not overwhelm a new learner with emergencies and stalls [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]. Insist on correct technique from the outset: it is much easier to build good habits than to fix faulty ones later [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

head: Stage
Straight-and-level content
rows: Ground

Objectives and what good looks like; seat adjustment; the nose and wingtip sight picture; control pressures and expected instrument indications [[24:67|AFH 3-6]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]; who has the controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
On the ramp
Learner seated in position on a marked centerline; mark vertical reference lines [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]
Demonstrate
Fly and explain: horizon, wingtips, quick instrument check, trim [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Learner tells, you fly
Hear whether the learner knows where to look before they are busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner flies
Practice in cruise; add horizontal reference lines in flight; then intentional power changes while holding level [[24:67|AFH 3-6]] [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]
Debrief
Learner assesses first, then your assessment with concrete fixes [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]

bullets: Keep it in the building blocks: hold straight-and-level until it is solid before combining it with turns, climbs and descents [[24:62|AFH 3-1]].
Do not grab the controls at the first error; when safe, let the learner go part way into the mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
If the performance looks good but you doubt the understanding, have the learner vary it slightly, for example changing airspeed with power while staying level [[25:182|AIH 9-12]] [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].
Make the learner do the scanning and clearing from day one; learners who think the instructor handles traffic never build the habit [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Teach one reference at a time on the first flight: nose, then wingtips, then the quick instrument check. Fixation is often a sign that a task has not had enough practice on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

check.q: On the first flight, why add horizontal windshield reference lines in the air rather than during the preflight?
check.a: Horizontal lines depend on the pitch attitudes actually flown, so the AFH says they are best made in flight, such as in cruise and slow flight [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

chunks.title: Risk: distractions, task priorities, awareness and disorientation

body.p: Distractions. Most stall and spin accidents happened when the pilot's attention was diverted from flying [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. The instructor teaches the learner to divide attention between a distracting task and aircraft control; examples include resetting the clock, reading the outside air temperature, finding a heading to an airport on a chart and identifying ground features [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. A distraction is momentary; an interruption makes the learner suspend one task for another and is a significant source of errors [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

Task prioritization. Individual tasks should be practiced until they can be done reasonably well in isolation before learners combine them [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Workload management means planning, prioritizing and sequencing tasks; when overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Once airborne, prioritizing tasks can buy the time to complete them without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

Loss of situational awareness. Situational awareness is the accurate perception of the factors that affect safety; fatigue, stress and work overload can fixate the pilot on one item, and many accidents begin with a minor distraction such as a gauge that is not reading right [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. It includes aircraft position, flightpath, the status of other aircraft and the environment [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

bullets: Gradual turn: a learner looking at a chart lets a wing drop, and anytime the wings are banked the airplane turns [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. A slow turn can go unnoticed; leveling afterward can cause the leans [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
Head movements: in a turn, a head movement can trigger the Coriolis illusion; retrieve dropped objects with minimal head movement [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
False horizon: it appears when the natural horizon is obscured or not readily apparent, for example over dark water at night [[24:65|AFH 3-4]] [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]].
No visible horizon is IMC for practical purposes, and a pilot without instrument training should avoid reduced visibility or night without a visible horizon [[24:65|AFH 3-4]] [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].
In visual conditions the eyes usually prevail over false sensations; take away the visual cues and false sensations can disorient a pilot quickly [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

callout.text: If you or the learner cannot hold attitude by the natural horizon, treat it as a genuine emergency, not as a chance to practice the instruments [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

check.q: You give a distraction during straight-and-level practice. Which kind keeps the Coriolis risk lowest?
check.a: One that needs little head movement, such as reading the outside air temperature, rather than reaching for an object; head movements in a turn can cause the Coriolis illusion [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

body.p: When weather permits, every pilot must keep vigilance to see and avoid other aircraft, under IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113]]. Most midair collisions and near midair collisions happen in good VFR weather, in daylight, within 5 miles of an airport and/or near navigation aids [[24:31|AFH 1-10]]. Collision avoidance, scanning and clearing are safety practices the instructor should stress from the very first dual flight [[24:31|AFH 1-10]].

bullets: Scan in short, regularly spaced eye movements of no more than 10°, looking at each area for at least 1 second [[24:32|AFH 1-11]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Eyes can need several seconds to refocus from the panel to distant objects [[24:32|AFH 1-11]].
No apparent relative motion means a likely collision course; no lateral or vertical motion but growing in size means take evasive action now [[24:32|AFH 1-11]] [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Above the horizon, the other aircraft is probably higher; below it, probably lower [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Move your head around blind spots and lift a wing when needed to see [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

body.p: Straight-and-level specifics: during sustained straight-and-level flight, execute clearing procedures at periodic intervals; make clearing turns before any practice maneuver, and during instruction have the learner call out 'clear left, right, above, and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Teach a clearing procedure and insist on its use [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. Traffic clusters near VORs, airways and surface areas, and haze, a dirty windshield and flying toward the sun all cut detection [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

callout.text: In one study of midair collisions, a flight instructor was aboard in 37 percent of the accidents [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Your attention is on the learner, so make the learner own the scan.

check.q: Your learner flies a long straight-and-level leg to the practice area. What does the PHAK say to do about traffic on that leg?
check.a: During sustained periods of straight-and-level flight, execute appropriate clearing procedures at periodic intervals [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

body.p: The AFH lists 11 common errors for straight-and-level flight [[24:70|AFH 3-9]] and adds a trim error [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]. The first beginner error to look for is a pitch or bank correction made while still looking inside [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. For S2 the examiner will fly some of these; name what you see, give the cause and give the fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Improper pitch and bank reference points on the airplane
A different nose point each time; altitude wanders
Set the references on the ground from the learner's own seat position, with tape or marker lines if needed [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]
Forgetting preselected reference points on later flights
The first minutes of each lesson start with drifting altitude
Recheck the seat and the reference before departure; have the learner describe it [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]
Setting or correcting attitude by the instruments, not the horizon
Head down while making corrections
Correct on the horizon, then glance in to confirm; the most common beginner error is correcting while still looking inside [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]
Chasing the flight instruments
A series of excessive corrections following the needles
Attitude flying: set the picture on the horizon, wait, then cross-check [[24:67|AFH 3-6]] [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]
Mechanically pushing or pulling the controls
Abrupt nose movements
Accurate, smooth pressures; the pressure gives the result, not the movement [[24:64|AFH 3-3]]
Not scanning outside for traffic, weather and terrain
Head still, eyes fixed in one direction
Scan both wingtips and the sky in 10° steps [[24:69|AFH 3-8]] [[24:32|AFH 1-11]]
Tight palm grip on the controls
Closed fist on the yoke, poor feel
Fingertips only; address it at the onset of training [[24:64|AFH 3-3]]
Overcontrolling
Constant control motion, nose bobbing
A trimmed airplane needs almost no pressure; make measured corrections [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]
Habitually flying one wing low, or holding direction with rudder only
One wingtip higher; rudder held against it
Make the wingtips the primary bank reference; correct with coordinated aileron and rudder [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]
No timely, measured input after a deviation
A small drift allowed to grow
Detect and correct small deviations early with minor control corrections [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]
Inadequate attention to sensory inputs for feel
Ignores a change in wind noise or engine sound
Teach perceiving and reacting to sound, vibration and forces [[24:64|AFH 3-3]]
Flying the airplane with the trim
Trim wheel used to change pitch, or pressure never trimmed out
Attitude first, held with pressure, then trim [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]

body.p: Analyze before you correct. When the learner thinks aloud while flying, you can tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Glance at the learner's eyes: a long stare at one instrument suggests fixation, and a gaze that never goes to the engine instruments suggests inattention [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Fixation often means the task needs more practice on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

callout.text: A learner who drags one wing and holds opposite rudder will struggle with every later maneuver [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]. Fix it in the first lessons, before VIII.B turns are introduced.

check.q: The heading holds steady but the left wingtip sits lower than the right and the ball is off center. Which listed error is this and what is the fix?
check.a: Flying one wing low and holding heading with rudder. Use the wingtips as the primary bank reference and level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder [[24:69|AFH 3-8]] [[24:70|AFH 3-9]].

The bottom two, labeled Natural horizon reference point, show a yellow dot on the horizon above the panel with enlarged instruments in front.

scenario.title: A first lesson on a hazy afternoon
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. Today's learner has never flown a light airplane and is visibly nervous. The trainer has a glass panel. The practice area is over a large lake, 8 miles from a VOR that two other flight schools use. Visibility is fine over land, but haze sits over the water and the horizon there is hard to see. The plan is straight-and-level flight with the learner on the controls.

questions.q: What do you do on the ramp before engine start, and why there?
questions.a: Adjust the seat so the learner sees over the panel and can fully depress the pedals, then set the nose reference and vertical lines with the airplane on a marked centerline, because the references depend on seat position, height and posture [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

questions.q: How do you handle the learner's nerves in the briefing?
questions.a: Treat the fear as normal, say what the flight will feel like, and keep the lesson positive rather than leading with emergencies [[25:45|AIH 2-12]] [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

questions.q: How do you introduce the glass display without creating a fixation?
questions.a: Brief the instrument indications along with the outside references from the first control briefing [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], then keep control outside with only brief checks inside, about 90 and 10 percent [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

questions.q: Over the lake the horizon disappears into haze. What do you do?
questions.a: With no visible horizon it is IMC for practical purposes and a false horizon is likely; move the practice back over land where the horizon is clear [[24:65|AFH 3-4]] [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]. Integrated instruction does not prepare the learner for IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

questions.q: How do you manage collision risk on the way out and during practice?
questions.a: Traffic clusters near VORs [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. Have the learner scan in 10° steps [[24:32|AFH 1-11]], clear periodically on long straight legs and call 'clear left, right, above, and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

questions.q: After 10 minutes the learner holds heading with right rudder while the left wing sits low. How do you analyze and fix it?
questions.a: Ask the learner to talk through what they see to separate a misconception from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Then point to both wingtips as the primary bank reference and level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

skills.do: Establish and maintain straight-and-level flight from the right seat while explaining the nose reference, the wingtips, the quick instrument cross-check and trim. The CFI ACS gives no numeric tolerance for this Task, so hold heading and altitude as precisely as you will expect a learner to.
skills.practice: Fly the talk-through aloud on every practice flight until talking costs you no altitude, and practice intentional power changes while holding level [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task: when the examiner flies an error such as chasing the instruments, one wing low with opposite rudder or a death grip, name it, explain the cause and give the fix.
skills.practice: Learn the 11 AFH errors and the trim error by heart with a 'what you see' and a fix for each, and rehearse with another CFI applicant flying them for you [[24:70|AFH 3-9]] [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

quiz.q: Per the AFH, what two things does a pilot maintain in straight-and-level flight?
options: Airspeed and altitude
Heading and altitude
Heading and airspeed
Pitch and power setting
quiz.why: Straight-and-level flight is flight in which heading and altitude are maintained [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

quiz.q: Bank attitude is the angle between the natural horizon and which line on the airplane?
options: The longitudinal axis, from the nose to the tail
The vertical axis through the center of gravity
The propeller thrust line
The lateral axis, wingtip to wingtip
quiz.why: Bank attitude uses the lateral axis, wingtip to wingtip [[24:65|AFH 3-4]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say a beginner loses by gripping the yoke with a closed palm?
options: The sensitive feel needed to develop 'feel'
Rudder authority at the low airspeeds of slow flight
The ability to use the trim wheel
Most of the elevator's travel
quiz.why: A closed palm grip loses the sensitive feeling that builds 'feel' of the airplane [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].

quiz.q: In an airplane with rudder, elevator and aileron trim, which order does the AFH give?
options: Elevator, then rudder, then aileron
Aileron, then elevator, then rudder
Elevator first, then aileron, then rudder
Rudder, then elevator, then aileron
quiz.why: The rudder is trimmed first, then elevator, then aileron [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

quiz.q: Placing the elevator trim control full nose-down moves a typical elevator trim tab where?
options: To its full up position
To its full down position
To neutral, with the stabilizer moving
Wherever the elevator happens to be
quiz.why: Full nose-down trim moves the tab full up; airflow forces the elevator trailing edge down and the nose drops [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].

quiz.q: Which seat position does the AFH call for when setting up the reference points?
options: As high as the seat will go, for the widest possible view of the horizon
Seeing over the panel while fully depressing the pedals without strain
Far enough back that the arms are fully straight with hands on the yoke
Whatever position the instructor uses in the right seat
quiz.why: Sit normally, seeing adequately over the panel while able to fully depress the rudder pedals without straining [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

quiz.q: Why does the AFH make the wingtips the primary reference for a level bank attitude?
options: They show the pitch attitude more clearly than the nose reference does
The nose's short reference line lets small bank errors go unseen
The attitude indicator is unreliable below cruise airspeed
Wingtips are the only part of the airplane visible in haze
quiz.why: Slight bank deviations go unnoticed on the nose's short horizontal line but are easily seen on the wingtips [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

quiz.q: Under integrated flight instruction, how much attention does the AFH put inside the flight deck?
options: Roughly one quarter of the time
About half, split evenly
About 90 percent, outside the rest
No more than about 10 percent
quiz.why: No more than about 10 percent of attention should be inside the flight deck [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

quiz.q: Per the PHAK, what reduces the chance of a Coriolis illusion when retrieving a dropped chart?
options: Retrieving it with minimal head movement
Leveling the wings with rudder alone first
Closing the eyes briefly during the reach
Trimming slightly nose up before reaching
quiz.why: Retrieve objects with minimal head movement and be alert for the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

quiz.q: During sustained straight-and-level flight, what does the PHAK say about clearing?
options: Gentle banks left and right at a frequency that permits continuous scanning
Clearing is needed only before turns, not on straight legs
Execute appropriate clearing procedures at periodic intervals
Clear once at the start of the leg, then rely on ATC
quiz.why: During sustained straight-and-level flight, execute appropriate clearing procedures at periodic intervals; gentle banks are for climbs and descents [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner keeps the altimeter needle within a few feet but makes a new pitch correction every second, each one larger than the last. What is happening and what is your fix?
options: Chasing the instruments; set pitch on the horizon, wait, then cross-check
Rough air; tell the learner to hold the controls more firmly to damp out the bumps
Mistrimmed elevator; add nose-up trim until the corrections stop by themselves
Altimeter lag; switch the learner to the vertical speed indicator
final_quiz.why: A beginner who flies by instrument indications, not understanding lag, ends up chasing them; control by the natural horizon and then cross-check [[24:67|AFH 3-6]] [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

final_quiz.q: Heading is steady, but the left wingtip sits lower against the horizon than the right one and the ball is off center. What is the most likely error?
options: A fuel imbalance that only aileron trim can cure
Flying one wing low and holding heading with opposite rudder
Parallax from the left seat, which is normal and needs no fix
A bent ground adjustable rudder tab that needs a mechanic
final_quiz.why: Habitually flying one wing low and holding direction with rudder is a listed error; the wingtips as the primary reference prevent it [[24:69|AFH 3-8]] [[24:70|AFH 3-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner raises the nose by rolling in nose-up trim and never holds back pressure. How do you correct the technique?
options: Accept it, since it gives smoother pitch changes than the yoke
Teach the learner to trim first and then fine tune the pitch with the yoke
Have the learner hold pressure only and skip trim until the next lesson
Set the attitude with elevator pressure first, then trim out the pressure
final_quiz.why: Flying the airplane with the trim is a common fault; establish and hold the attitude with control pressure, then trim it out [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

final_quiz.q: On her third lesson a learner flies level well in the first minutes, but you see the seat is two notches lower than last time. What should you check first?
options: The altimeter setting from the last weather report she got
The seat position and the nose reference she is using
The elevator trim indicator's takeoff mark
Her grip on the yoke and how tightly she is holding it
final_quiz.why: Reference points depend on seating position, height and posture, and forgetting or misusing reference points is a listed error [[24:67|AFH 3-6]] [[24:70|AFH 3-9]].

final_quiz.q: Over a flat, snow covered valley your learner cannot hold a straight line. What does the AFH tell the pilot to rely on?
options: A point on the far horizon only
The turn coordinator's ball
The magnetic heading indication
The shadow of the airplane on the snow
final_quiz.why: Surface points do not work over flat snow covered surfaces; rely on the magnetic heading indication [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

final_quiz.q: The haze over the ocean leaves no visible horizon, and your learner suggests 'practicing on the instruments' for a while. What is the right response?
options: Agree, since integrated training builds exactly the instrument skill needed here
Agree, but only if the learner keeps the wings level on the PFD
Decline: this is IMC for practical purposes; turn toward a visible horizon
Decline, and have the learner close their eyes to feel the airplane instead
final_quiz.why: No visible horizon is IMC for practical and safety purposes [[24:65|AFH 3-4]], and integrated instruction does not prepare a pilot for IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: A learner says the attitude indicator is easier than the horizon, so why bother looking out? Which AFH point best answers this?
options: The attitude indicator is required to be cross-checked only during night flight
The horizon gives immediate indications many times larger than any instrument
The attitude indicator works only above cruise power
The horizon is required by the ACS as the reference for every visual maneuver
final_quiz.why: Attitude by reference to the natural horizon presents immediate and accurate indications many times larger than on any instrument [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: During your right seat demonstration, you notice the learner's eyes stay on the PFD for 20 seconds at a time. What does this most likely show, and what can you do?
options: Inattention to the engine gauges; brief an engine scan
Normal workload for a first lesson; no action is needed from the instructor yet
Motion sickness; return to the airport at once
Fixation on the instruments; covering them for a time is an option
final_quiz.why: A long stare at one instrument suggests fixation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]], and the AFH allows instrument covers for the first several hours to force outside references [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner sets lower power for a slower cruise and wants to stay at the same altitude. What must happen to angle of attack and what extra care is needed?
options: Angle of attack decreases; watch for an overspeed as the nose comes down
Angle of attack stays the same; just retrim for the new airspeed
Angle of attack increases; watch the margin to the critical angle
Angle of attack increases; the stall speed then drops
final_quiz.why: As thrust and airspeed decrease the angle of attack must increase to hold altitude, so extra vigilance is needed near the critical angle of attack [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: You ask a learner to compute true airspeed during straight-and-level practice, and the heading drifts 30° before she notices. What does the AIH suggest about the cause?
options: The heading indicator has precessed and needs resetting to the magnetic compass
Straight-and-level is not yet practiced enough to combine with other tasks
The distraction was unrealistic and should not be used
She needs more rudder trim before any distraction
final_quiz.why: Tasks should be performed reasonably well in isolation before being combined; fixation on a task is often a sign it has not had enough practice [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

final_quiz.q: Ahead and slightly right, another airplane stays in the same spot on the windshield and is growing larger. What should you teach the learner to do?
options: Hold heading; it is probably passing well behind
Take immediate evasive action
Climb to get it below the horizon, then reassess
Wait to see if it shows lateral movement
final_quiz.why: No lateral or vertical motion but increasing in size means take immediate evasive action [[24:32|AFH 1-11]] [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies straight-and-level perfectly, but you suspect it is copied from your demonstration without understanding. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Repeat the same demonstration until the learner can recite each step aloud
Sign off the maneuver, since the performance meets the standard
Ask the learner to write the procedure out after the flight
Have the learner vary it slightly or combine it with other operations
final_quiz.why: Learners who may not understand the principles should be asked to vary the maneuver slightly, combine it with other operations, or apply its elements elsewhere [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: On the first lesson your learner is tense, grips hard and asks what happens if the engine quits. What is the best response from the AIH?
options: Demonstrate a power-off glide right away to prove that the airplane still flies
Treat the fear as normal, explain what to expect, and keep the lesson positive
Change the subject so the learner focuses on the lesson plan
Cut the lesson short and schedule more ground school first
final_quiz.why: Treat fears as normal, tell learners what to expect, and present the first lessons positively rather than with emergencies [[25:45|AIH 2-12]] [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

takeaways: Straight-and-level means heading and altitude held; every other fundamental is a variation of it.
Set the seat and the reference points on the ground, from the learner's own seat.
Nose on the horizon for pitch, both wingtips for bank; correct with coordinated aileron and rudder.
Attitude first, held with light fingertip pressure, then trim the pressure out.
Integrated from the first briefing: about 90 percent outside, brief checks inside, and never a substitute for IMC training.
Make the learner own the scan and the clearing, including periodic clearing on long straight legs.
Know the 11 AFH errors plus the trim error, what each looks like, and the fix.
cfi_notes: The AFH 3-9 common errors list is garbled in the printed handbook: item 1 reads 'improper pitch and bank refe...equent flights' and item 11 ends 'feel for t...rence points on the airplane to establish attitude' [[24:70|AFH 3-9]]. Read together, item 1 is improper pitch and bank reference points on the airplane to establish attitude, and item 11 is inadequate attention to sensory inputs in developing feel for the airplane. This lesson teaches that reading; check the next AFH revision.

The AFH lets instructors cover the flight instruments for the first several hours [[24:67|AFH 3-6]], while the AIH says instrument references should begin the first time each maneuver is introduced [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Both can be true: brief and show the instruments from the start, and use covers only to break a fixation habit.

The CFI ACS gives no numeric tolerance for AI.VIII.A. Do not borrow the instrument-reference numbers from other Tasks as the standard for a first-lesson learner; the AIH says to base assessment on standards suitably modified to the learner's stage [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

The AFH says trim the rudder first, then elevator, then aileron, but also that trimming rudder and aileron while airspeed varies is impractical [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]. Teach 'stabilize the speed and pitch first, then trim in that order.'

Every AFH sight picture is described from the left seat [[24:69|AFH 3-8]] [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. The sources are silent on how the picture looks from the right seat; build the learner's references from the left seat, not from yours.

The AIH distraction list includes dropping a pencil and getting something from the back seat [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], while the PHAK warns that head movements can trigger the Coriolis illusion in a turn [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Give those in straight-and-level flight, never mid turn, and prefer the low head movement ones with a nervous learner.

The 90 and 10 percent split is approximate in the AFH ('approximately 90 percent', 'no more than about 10 percent') [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. Teach it as a habit to aim for, not something to time.
The AFH expects the instructor to know AC 90-48 and the AIM on scanning and collision avoidance [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. This lesson cites the AIM; read the AC before teaching scanning in depth.
gaps: Cruise power settings, the level pitch attitude in degrees and trim positions for a given airplane come from the POH/AFM; the handbooks give none.
No source here gives a numeric tolerance for visual straight-and-level flight in this Task.
The sources do not say how long windshield tape or marker lines should stay, beyond 'a short period', or whether they hamper the traffic scan [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
No source describes the right seat sight picture or a right seat demonstration technique for this maneuver.
The AFH does not say how many hours 'the first several hours' with instrument covers means [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

activities.title: What is the airplane telling you?
activities.intro: Tap a cue, then tap what it most likely means.

pairs.r: Increased G, like a bank or a pull-up
The airplane is slipping or skidding

activities.title: Trim it the AFH way
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order for an airplane with rudder, elevator and aileron trim, then tap Check.
steps: Set the attitude and power, and hold the attitude with control pressure
Let the airspeed and pitch attitude become constant
Hold the wings level with aileron while trimming out rudder pressure
Trim out any remaining aileron pressure
Relax the pressure and confirm the airplane holds the attitude

activities.title: Ground or air?
activities.intro: Tap each setup step, then tap where the AFH says it is best done.

items.t: Adjust the seat to see over the panel and reach full rudder
Mark vertical reference lines on the windshield
Mark horizontal reference lines for cruise
Mark horizontal reference lines for slow flight
Set the nose reference with the airplane on a marked centerline
Check the nose point against altitude trend on the altimeter

activities.title: Find the straight-and-level references
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the picture.

pins.label: Natural horizon seen past the left wing
Natural horizon seen past the right wing
Shows whether the heading has drifted
Confirms the altitude is being held
Glass attitude display: wings against the horizon

activities.title: True or false: integrated instruction
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Integrated flight instruction prepares a learner to continue flight into IMC.
cards.why: False. It does not prepare pilots for IMC, and the instructor must make that clear [[24:67|AFH 3-6]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

cards.s: The control inputs are different depending on whether the learner uses outside or instrument references.
cards.why: False. No distinction in the operation of the controls is permitted [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

cards.s: A pitch change of several inches on the horizon can look almost insignificant on the attitude indicator.
cards.why: True. That is why the horizon is the primary reference [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

cards.s: Integrated instruction starts with the first briefing on the function of the flight controls.
cards.why: True. That briefing includes the instrument indications and the outside references [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

cards.s: Failing to integrate visual and instrument references shortens the training needed for a private certificate.
cards.why: False. It lengthens the instruction needed [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

activities.title: Numbers worth briefing
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A learner looks down at a chart and lets a wing drop. The airplane turns at 1.5° per second for 2 minutes before anyone notices. How many degrees has the heading changed?
items.why: 2 minutes = 120 seconds. 1.5 x 120 = 180°. Anytime the wings are banked, the airplane turns [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

items.q: Scanning a 180° field in eye movements of 10°, looking at each area for 1 second, how many seconds does one sweep take at least?
items.why: 180 / 10 = 18 areas. 18 x 1 second = 18 seconds. Movements of no more than 10°, each area at least 1 second [[24:32|AFH 1-11]].

items.q: Using the AFH limit of no more than about 10 percent of attention inside, about how many seconds of each minute should a learner spend looking inside?
items.why: 60 seconds x 0.10 = 6 seconds. No more than about 10 percent inside [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

items.q: An airplane in steady level flight at 100 knots accelerates to 200 knots. By what factor does the power to overcome parasite drag grow?
items.why: Speed ratio 200 / 100 = 2. Parasite drag grows with the square, 2 x 2 = 4, and power with the cube, 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, as the PHAK states [[1:261|PHAK 11-5]].

activities.title: First lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are a new CFI with a learner on the first flight lesson in a high-wing trainer. The practice area is over farmland next to a large lake.

steps.s: Before engine start the learner, who is short, can barely see over the glareshield.
options: Leave it; the view improves once airborne
Adjust the seat so she sees over the panel and still reaches full rudder travel
Have her sit forward on the seat edge during the lesson
Let her use your reference point from the right seat
steps.why: The seat is adjusted to see adequately over the panel while fully depressing the pedals without straining, and the references depend on seating position, height and posture [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

steps.s: In cruise you want a horizontal reference line on the windshield for level flight.
options: Draw it now, in cruise, with the learner seated normally
Wait and draw it after landing on the ramp
Skip it; horizontal lines are only for slow flight
Draw it from your own eye level in the right seat
steps.why: Horizontal reference lines are best established in flight, such as in cruise and slow flight configurations [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

steps.s: The learner keeps looking out the left side, and the left wing slowly drops.
options: Tell her to look only at the attitude indicator
Have her scan both wingtips against the horizon
Trim left aileron to stop the drift
Ignore it; a slight bank does not change heading
steps.why: Looking to one side causes unconscious pressure that way; scanning both wingtips is the only positive check for level wings [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

steps.s: Twenty minutes into a long straight leg, neither of you has looked for traffic since the clearing turns.
options: Keep going; you cleared at the start
Make gentle S-turns continuously until landing
Clear again now and at periodic intervals, with the learner calling it
Ask ATC to watch for traffic so you can keep teaching
steps.why: During sustained straight-and-level flight, clear at periodic intervals and have the learner verbalize the clearing [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

steps.s: You turn over the lake and the hazy horizon blends into the water.
options: Continue; it is good attitude instrument practice
Turn back over land where the horizon is clear
Descend so the shoreline gives a horizon
Have the learner fly by feel for a minute
steps.why: Haze over water with no visible horizon is IMC for practical purposes [[24:65|AFH 3-4]]; integrated training does not prepare the learner for IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
